source_caption:
To this day, one of the greatest motivational movies ever made. 🥊

When Stallone wrote Rocky in 1975, he was a struggling actor with very little money. According to the New York Times, he wrote the screenplay in just three and a half days, with only $106 in his wallet.

Around that time, Stallone watched Muhammad Ali fight Chuck Wepner, a largely unknown heavyweight who was expected to be easily beaten. Instead, Wepner knocked Ali down and lasted until the 15th round before losing by TKO with only 19 seconds left. Stallone later described the fight as a powerful metaphor for life, and it became one of the inspirations for Rocky. 

Stallone’s real-life struggles also make Rocky’s story feel strangely personal. He was trying to make it in Hollywood, taking small acting jobs and struggling financially while waiting for his big break.

When producers became interested in his script, Stallone insisted on playing Rocky himself. He turned down opportunities to simply sell the screenplay because he wanted to be the one to bring the character to life.

And it paid off.

Made for around $1 million and shot in just 28 days, Rocky became a huge success. It received 10 Academy Award nominations and won three, including Best Picture, Directing and Film Editing. Stallone was also nominated for both Best Actor and Original Screenplay.

That’s why Rocky feels like more than just a boxing movie.

Rocky was a nobody who finally got his chance.

Stallone was, in many ways, doing the same thing.

He wrote a story about an overlooked fighter refusing to give up — while fighting for his own chance to be seen.
